newsitem.title: JAPAN: Noted Japanese author Shusaku Endo dies at 73.
newsitem.headline: Noted Japanese author Shusaku Endo dies at 73.

text.p: Novelist Shusaku Endo, one of Japan's best-known novelists and winner of virtually every major Japanese literary award, died on Sunday at the age of 73, his family said.
Endo won international acclaim with his works. Critics said that as a Roman Catholic, he offered a unique view of Japan to the outside world.
He was known at home as both a serious author of novels and plays on religious themes and as a humorist.
Doctors at the Tokyo hospital in which he was staying said that he died from respiratory complications caused by hepatitis.
Born in Tokyo, Endo grew up in China, returning to Japan with his mother in 1933 after his parents were divorced.

Poor health kept him from military service during World War Two. He majored in French literature at Tokyo's Keio University and in 1950 became one of the first Japanese to study abroad after the war, spending two and a half years at the University of Lyon in France.
Soon after his return to Japan, Endo began his career as a novelist,
"Shiroi Hito" (White Man) published in 1955, brought him the prestigious Akutagawa Prize.

In "Umi to Dokuyaku" (1957), published in English as "The Sea and Poison" in 1972, Endo lashes out at the lack of moral conscience that allowed Japanese doctors to perform experiments on a captured American pilot during the war.

Another prize-winning work, "Chimmoku" (1966), published in English as "Silence" in 1969, studied the persecution of 17th-century Japanese Christians. In the book, Endo showed the conflict he said he felt as a Japanese person embracing a foreign religion.
